scenes.name: Naked funk: la era Reagan
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La era del naked funk abarca las cimas de Prince, Michael Jackson y los dos mandatos de Reagan: recortes, desindustrialización, millones de sin techo, la «guerra contra las drogas» en lugar de contra la pobreza y, desde 1982, el crack. La música negra se volvió narcisista y escapista, del «yo primero»; las bandas, demasiado caras para la ciudad. La industria ofrecía estereotipos (banda pop, crooner, banda funk guarra, según Jon Pareles), MTV no ponía vídeos negros hasta Thriller y Jackson y Prince marcaron las cuotas del crossover. En 1975 trece números 1 R&B eran funk; en 1985 diecisiete de veinte eran baladas. Warner echó a Clinton y CBS sepultó «Pumpin’ It Up»; murieron o se convirtieron Hathaway, Joe Tex, Marvin Gaye, Al Green, Larry Graham. Las máquinas sustituyeron vientos, órgano (el Yamaha DX7), batería y bajo: solo sobrevivió la guitarra rítmica sobre el bajo sintetizado y la palmada electrónica. La insinuación dejó paso al sexo explícito sin cerebro («Do Me Baby», «Beep a Freak»), y llegaron el bass de Miami (2 Live Crew), Egyptian Lover, el New Jack Swing de Teddy Riley y la farsa de Milli Vanilli. Los funkers de verdad abandonaron la radio: el underground (hip hop, go-go) llevó el funk adelante.

podcast.title: Benchmark for Innovation
podcast.body: His significant impact on guitar technique and technology in the late 1970s and early 1980s is used as a point of comparison for Matt Bellamy's influence in the 2000s. "What Eddie Van Halen was to the late 1970s and early 1980s, you could say that Matt is the equivalent to the 2000s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Constantly Modified Frankenstrat
podcast.body: Eddie Van Halen's famous Frankenstrat guitar was subject to continuous modifications. He persistently altered the instrument in his relentless pursuit of the specific guitar tones he envisioned in his mind. "Think of Eddie Van Halen's Frankenstrat, which was always being modified as Eddie chased the guitar tones he heard in his head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Frankenstein Guitar
podcast.body: Eddie Van Halen's "Frankenstein" guitar is essentially a heavily modified Fender Stratocaster, showcasing his innovative approach to instrument customization. "and Eddie Van Halen's Frankenstein guitar, that's basically a heavily modified Stratocaster."

podcast.title: Pioneering Electric Guitar Techniques
podcast.body: Eddie Van Halen is recognized for being among the first to perform innovative actions with an electric guitar, pushing the boundaries of what was thought possible with the instrument. His contributions were revolutionary and influential in the development of guitar playing. "Jimmy Hendrix and Eddie Van Halen were the first to do things with an electric guitar that no one else had."

xref.title: Three Lead Singers – David Lee Roth, Sammy Hagar, Gary Cherone; Eddie Van Halen Died October 6, 2020
xref.body: Van Halen has had three lead singers: David Lee Roth (1973–1984), Sammy Hagar (1985–1996), Roth briefly in late 1996, Gary Cherone of Extreme (1996–1999), Hagar again (2003–2005), and Roth from 2006 onward. A reunion tour with Roth was being planned when Eddie Van Halen was diagnosed with cancer; he died on October 6, 2020. "And then Eddie Van Halen got sick with cancer and eventually died on October 6, 2020."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: At Least 11 Different Lead Singers Over the Band's History
xref.body: Black Sabbath's vocal history is extraordinarily convoluted: Ozzy Osbourne (1968–1977), Dave Walker (briefly 1977–78), Ronnie James Dio (1979–1982), Ian Gillan (1982–1984), Ron Keel and Dave DeNato (both 1984), Jeff Fenholt (1985), Ozzy briefly (1985), Glenn Hughes (1985–1986), Ray Gillan (1986–1987), Tony Martin (1987–1991), Ozzy returned (1992), Tony Martin again (1993–1997), Ozzy from 1997 through various reunion configurations until Eddie Van Halen— no, that's a different band. By conservative count, at least 11 different people have fronted Black Sabbath. "By my count, at least 11 different lead singers for one band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Comparison to Eddie Van Halen and Tapping Technique
xref.body: Marnie Stern is often compared to Eddie Van Halen due to her distinctive guitar style, which notably incorporates the tapping technique. "If there's a female version of Eddie Van Halen, it might be Marney Stern. Like Eddie, she employs tapping into her style."

xref.title: High-Profile Touring Guitarist
xref.body: Jennifer Batten toured with Michael Jackson and was specifically tasked with playing Eddie Van Halen's guitar parts from the song "Beat It" during Jackson's live performances. "Jennifer Batten, who toured with Michael Jackson, played Eddie Van Halens parts on Beated when Jackson played live."

xref.title: Pioneering Electric Guitar Techniques
xref.body: Jimmy Hendrix is credited as one of the first artists to introduce groundbreaking techniques and sounds with the electric guitar. His innovations expanded the expressive capabilities of the instrument, setting new standards for guitarists.
